new_statements.quote: La tonalidad en el Tnu’un Savi es una de las características fonológicas más destacables del idioma, si no se pronuncia de manera adecuada o no se relaciona contextualmente algún concepto con lo que se quiere enunciar podríamos expresar o entender una cosa por otra. [fn. 23: En este capítulo se hace uso de Tnu’un Savi para nombrar el idioma de la lluvia, Tnu’un hace referencia a la “palabra” en la variante lingüística de Santa María Yosoyúa ...] ... Si escucháramos la palabra yaà podríamos identificar un alargamiento de la vocal a con un ligero tono que baja de medio a grave, por ello se le ha representado gráficamente a la segunda à con una tilde ortográfica grave. [fn. 25: Los ejemplos utilizados en este cuadro se representan con la variante lingüística que estuve estudiando de Santa María Yukuhiti.]
new_statements.translation: Tonality in Tnu'un Savi is one of the most notable phonological characteristics of the language; if it is not pronounced properly, or a concept is not related contextually to what one means to say, we could express or understand one thing for another. [fn. 23: In this chapter Tnu'un Savi is used to name the language of the rain; Tnu'un refers to the 'word' in the linguistic variant of Santa María Yosoyúa ...] ... If we listened to the word yaà we could identify a lengthening of the vowel a with a slight tone falling from mid to low, which is why the second à has been written with a grave accent. [fn. 25: The examples in this table are given in the variant I was studying, that of Santa María Yukuhiti.]
new_statements.citation: Quintero Báez, Ana Itzel. 2026. Yaà Yáá / Música de mi lengua, de Ve'e Ñuu a Nundaa Ka'anu Ñuu Yuva; procesos colaborativos para la revitalización lingüística del Tù'ùn Savi. Tesis de Maestría en Antropología Social, Centro de Investigaciones y Estudios Superiores en Antropología Social (CIESAS), Ciudad de México, abril de 2026. 136 pp. Director: José Antonio Flores Farfán. Repositorio CIESAS hdl 1015/1955.
new_statements.locator: Capítulo 5 'Yaá Yàà Tnu'un Savi, Nundaa Ka'anu Ñuu Yu'uva', printed pp. 86-87 (pp. 91-92), with footnotes 23-25; tone table p. 87
new_statements.relation_note: States only that tonality is one of the most salient phonological traits of Tnu'un Savi (the language named in its Yosoyúa form), such that mispronounced tone changes meaning; describes the word yaà as a lengthened vowel with a slight mid-to-low falling tone written with a grave accent, and lists vowel length, glottalization and 'modulación tonal' as the phonological resources of the language. No tone inventory, no sandhi, nothing on stress/acento; the illustrative tone set is from the Yukuhiti variant, not Yosoyúa/Tijaltepec. A lay, family-level remark, not an analysis.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexical tone is contrastive (tone language); no word-stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Social-anthropology MA thesis (not a linguistic description) on arts/music-based revitalization; the action-research chapters (4-5) were carried out in Nundaa Ka'anu / Llano Grande, Buenavista and Guadalupe, agencias of Santa María Yosoyúa, Tlaxiaco region — the second town of Ethnologue/Glottolog's Tijaltepec Mixtec [xtl] (INALI lists 'mixteco de Santa María Yosoyúa' as its own variant beside 'de San Pablo Tijaltepec'). Main collaborator Audelia Hernández López is 'hablante de Tnu'un Savi, variante de Guadalupe, Santa María Yosoyúa' (p. 7); fn. 8 and fn. 23 define Tnu'un Savi / Sa'an Savi as the Santa María Yosoyúa variant names. CAVEAT: the author learnt the Santa María Yukuhiti variant (Tù'ùn Savi, Southwestern Tlaxiaco Mixtec [meh]); the tone minimal-set table on p. 87 (yaà 'música' / yáá 'lengua' / yàà 'blanco' / yaa 'ceniza' / ya'a 'chile') is explicitly in the Yukuhiti variant (fn. 25) and the Anexo 'Taller de Tù'ùn Savi' grammar notes (VSO, sixth vowel ɨ, N- past prefix, aspect paradigms) are 'Miramar Yucuhiti'. Yosoyúa-specific linguistic content is limited to the generic tonality remark, a handful of lexical items (vilu 'gato', linki 'ratón', chikuaku 'lagartija', koo 'serpiente', ña'aña), the note that Tnu'un Savi vs Sa'an Savi are everyday vs ceremonial registers in Yosoyúa (pp. 23-24), and a teacher's remark that Buenavista Yosoyúa speech differs considerably from his own variant (p. 114).
